transcriptClaims.claim:
**Yeah, I like it. This is substantially more than chair shuffling.** I read the full design and integration audit, then followed the current runtime, resolver, dispatch, capability fold, shared stream/result code, and representative tests.

The useful changes are concrete:

- **The package boundary does real work.** It depends on contracts and kit, receives persistence through ports, and exports one entry point. That makes inference independently exercisable without importing the server’s database or composition machinery. [package.json](/home/inktomi/inktomi-stack/development/orbweaver/packages/inference/package.json:10)
- **Providers and transports are finally different concepts.** Another compatible endpoint can be a provider row with features instead of another backend carrying slightly different history, retry, and parsing code. That reduces the number of places future fixes must land.
- **Selection has one executable home.** The binding fold, capability synthesis, and task dispatch are separate, understandable steps. Role clients resolve again at call time, so changing a binding affects the next call. [role-clients.ts](/home/inktomi/inktomi-stack/development/orbweaver/packages/inference/src/roles/role-clients.ts:105)
- **Normalization now preserves meaningful distinctions.** Requested versus applied settings, measured versus estimated cost, raw versus normalized termination, and replayable reasoning are actual behavioral improvements. The shared reducer’s handling of SDK-synthesized finishes is exactly the sort of defect one common implementation can prevent across transports. [stream.ts](/home/inktomi/inktomi-stack/development/orbweaver/packages/inference/src/backends/v4/stream.ts:234)

The conformance suite is particularly valuable: it tests whether different backends honor the same behavior, and makes missing drivers fail instead of quietly skipping coverage. That gives the abstraction teeth beyond matching method names.

**One concrete seam still looks unfinished:** background permission doesn’t appear enforced on the role-client execution path. Resolution emits a warning when `allowBackground` is false; `live()` takes only `resolved`, discarding that warning, and proceeds to the executor. Availability refuses it, but these calls don’t pass through availability. So switching background work off after binding appears insufficient to stop subsequent role-client calls. I traced this in source; I haven’t run a reproduction. [resolver](/home/inktomi/inktomi-stack/development/orbweaver/packages/inference/src/resolve/resolve-task.ts:281), [caller](/home/inktomi/inktomi-stack/development/orbweaver/packages/inference/src/roles/role-clients.ts:113)

My other criticism is the **documentation’s accumulated history**: the design mixes original requirements, superseded decisions, and later corrections. The code is considerably easier to understand than the document now. Once the remaining work settles, a concise account of the implemented architecture would help future readers avoid rebuilding something you deliberately removed.

I’d keep this architecture. Its payoff is fewer independent decisions and fewer duplicated implementations—not merely a cleaner directory tree. This was a read-only architectural assessment, not a fresh test or launch-certification run.

Yes — those are separate laundering mechanisms and they belong in the same audit.

The important additions are:

- **Indexed/element-access types** such as `RouterOutputs["chat"]["room"]` or `SomeMap[keyof SomeMap]`. They can correctly project a canonical type, but they can also make provenance disappear: the resulting type looks trusted while nobody checks how the runtime value entered the map.
- **The tRPC client/server bridge.** `inferRouterInputs` and `inferRouterOutputs` derive client types from the server router, but that only proves compile-time agreement. We must verify the actual input parser, output construction, serializer/transformer, and any client-side casts or schema twins. Type-only linkage does not validate server output.
- **Zod input/output divergence.** `z.input<T>`, `z.output<T>`, and `z.infer<T>` can differ when schemas use `transform`, `preprocess`, `coerce`, `catch`, `default`, `pipe`, or branded outputs. transcriptClaims.claim:
Probably **faster for some queries, but it cannot replace our `ts-morph` substrate yet**.

The repo already uses the sensible hybrid:

- `pnpm exec tsc` resolves to the native `ts7` package at 7.0.2 for compilation.
- `ts-morph` still runs against the JavaScript TypeScript 6.0.3 API for AST/checker work.
- `pnpm ast` uses `ts-morph` across 49 files and depends on arbitrary operations such as symbol resolution, alias origins, assignability, AST ancestry, declaration enumeration, and `findReferencesAsNodes()`.

Upstream currently labels the native LSP “nearly complete,” but the general API is still **not ready**. Their 7.1 API roadmap explicitly lists `createProgram` and `createSourceFile` as missing pieces needed by tools such as `ts-morph`. [typescript-go status](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/blob/main/README.md), [API roadmap](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/issues/4830).

Where native LSP could help:

- `refs`, rename-like identity lookup, definitions, and perhaps targeted callers.
- Repeated interactive queries against one warm server.
- Avoiding repeated project construction for one-symbol navigation.

Where it currently does not fit:

- `columns`, `respell`, `regkeys`, `stringy`, brand analysis, schema twins, arbitrary AST classification, and custom graph construction.
- One-shot CLI runs where LSP startup and JSON-RPC transfer may erase the speed gain.
- In-memory planted controls, because the native API’s ad hoc program/source-file surface is still being built.

So I would **not migrate `pnpm ast` to LSP wholesale**. The right experiment is a narrow benchmark adapter for `refs`/identity callers against a persistent TS7 LSP, measuring cold start, warm query, memory, and result parity. If that wins, we can use LSP as a navigation accelerator while keeping `ts-morph` for semantic audits. TypeScript’s own guidance still recommends side-by-side native compilation and the older API for tooling that needs it. [TypeScript 7 progress](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/progress-on-typescript-7-december-2025/)

I found a real reason the Code Mod Kit tests were behaving “weird” under commits. Git exports repository variables to hooks; the static hook launches tooling tests with those variables still present. Confirmed AST diagnostic mismatch:

- `chains` treats any reasoned `@public` as a ratified alive root, while the ratchet rejects bare `@public <reason>`.
- `dead` similarly reports any parsed bare marker as `TAGGED-KEEP`.

The dominant problem is repeated language-service reference search, multiplied by native worlds and by every value export.

Let:

- `F` = authored files,
- `P` = native programs,
- `E` = exported value declarations in package scope,
- `C(d)` = programs containing declaration `d`,
- `S(p)` = compiler graph size for program `p`,
- `R(d,p)` = references returned for `d` in `p`.

Current cost is approximately:

```text
load:       Θ(Σp S(p)) time and retained memory
enumerate:  Θ(F × P × membership-scan) plus export-map work
references: Θ(Σd∈E [P + Σp∈C(d) (S(p) + R(d,p))])
dedupe:     Θ(Σd references(d)) space, plus O(Ud log Ud) sort per declaration
```

`findReferencesAsNodes()` is implementation-dependent, but its worst-case search is program-wide. The important concrete fact is that it runs once per value export per containing native program.

Evidence:

- `collectTypeOnlyCandidates` visits every non-test in-scope file and every own export; no cheap candidate narrowing occurs before reference search: `tooling/src/ast/ops/typeonly.ts:157-171`.
- Every reference-findable value declaration immediately calls `semanticReferenceNodes`: `typeonly.ts:177-200`.
- `semanticReferenceNodes` delegates to workspace-wide `findReferences`: `tooling/src/_shared/ts-workspace.ts:106-113`.
- For each declaration, `findReferences`:
  - recomputes containing programs,
  - remaps the physical declaration by start/width,
  - runs `findReferencesAsNodes()` in every containing program,
  - canonicalizes and deduplicates only after all searches have happened,
  - sorts the complete union: `ts-workspace.ts:180-197`.
- `containingPrograms` scans every program and asks each retained `Project` for the file on every declaration: `ts-workspace.ts:168-171`.
- Native programs are separate retained `Project`s. Each loads its roots, resolves dependencies, and remains cached: `ts-workspace.ts:66-76`, `79-97`. Shared sources therefore occupy memory once per native program graph.
- Exact physical dedupe happens after the duplicated checker work, keyed by canonical path/start/end: `ts-workspace.ts:184-196`.
- The caller’s early `return` on a value reference occurs only after `semanticReferenceNodes` has already materialized the full all-world union: `typeonly.ts:181-200`.

The load/per-symbol split is empirically clear even though the CLI does not instrument those phases separately:

- `beginRun` occurs before `loadProject`, and `finishRun` only after the synchronous verb completes: `tooling/src/ast/cli.ts:127-139`.
- The ledger records scope/count/status but no clock: `tooling/src/ast/lib/ledger.ts:66-80`, `148-179`.
- JSON and narration are emitted after collection, so the zero-byte stdout during the run did not locate progress inside the candidate loop: `typeonly.ts:272-286`.
- The existing one-symbol native `refs createCodemodProject` timing was `34.25s` and `7,364,364 KB` peak RSS (`/tmp/world-tools-native-refs.time:3-12`).
- The full type-only run was `35:30.13` and `15,377,044 KB`. Thus roughly the first half-minute / 7.4 GB is native program construction plus one reference query; almost 35 additional minutes are repeated per-export searches. The additional heap is consistent with checker/reference caches and ts-morph wrappers retained across thousands of searches. This is an inference from comparable existing receipts, since the CLI has no phase timers.

There are several available caches, but none attacks the main multiplier:

- Each native `Project` is already lazy and cached (`ts-workspace.ts:85-94`).
- `sourceCorpus` is cached as an object (`ts-workspace.ts:163`, `206-248`), but its `getSourceFiles()` rebuilds the authored array and reruns `primaryConfig` for every path each call (`225-236`).
- `cmdTypeOnly` causes at least three corpus enumerations: scan, candidate collection, and stale-marker pass (`typeonly.ts:274-276`, `157-171`, `240-255`).
- `primaryConfig` repeatedly filters descriptors and performs linear `files.includes` membership searches (`ts-workspace.ts:144-152`).
- `containingPrograms` has no per-path memo (`168-171`).
- `findReferences` has no per-declaration memo. Adding a full reference-result cache would likely worsen the 15 GB heap and gives little benefit here because each declaration is normally queried once.
- Liveness is not a safe import-level prefilter. It deliberately marks named imports regardless of whether the binding is used at a type or value position (`tooling/src/ast/lib/liveness.ts:52-77`, `346-361`). The type-only controls explicitly require a plain value imp…

Yes — those are separate laundering mechanisms and they belong in the same audit.

The important additions are:

- **Indexed/element-access types** such as `RouterOutputs["chat"]["room"]` or `SomeMap[keyof SomeMap]`. They can correctly project a canonical type, but they can also make provenance disappear: the resulting type looks trusted while nobody checks how the runtime value entered the map.
- **The tRPC client/server bridge.** `inferRouterInputs` and `inferRouterOutputs` derive client types from the server router, but that only proves compile-time agreement. We must verify the actual input parser, output construction, serializer/transformer, and any client-side casts or schema twins. Type-only linkage does not validate server output.
- **Zod input/output divergence.** `z.input<T>`, `z.output<T>`, and `z.infer<T>` can differ when schemas use `transform`, `preprocess`, `coerce`, `catch`, `default`, `pipe`, or branded outputs. A value can be accepted as a plain string and emerge typed as something stronger; that is safe only when the transform actually validates or constructs that stronger value.
- **Result-driven narrowing.** `safeParse().success`, discriminated unions, assertion functions, and generic helpers can either establish a type or merely convince the compiler they did. We need to follow the returned value, not just see that Zod appears somewhere nearby.

I’m adding those exact families to the closed denominator for **#2531**, including the single client→server router type bridge and every Zod schema whose input and output types differ.

transcriptIngestionBacklog.claim:
Probably **faster for some queries, but it cannot replace our `ts-morph` substrate yet**.

The repo already uses the sensible hybrid:

- `pnpm exec tsc` resolves to the native `ts7` package at 7.0.2 for compilation.
- `ts-morph` still runs against the JavaScript TypeScript 6.0.3 API for AST/checker work.
- `pnpm ast` uses `ts-morph` across 49 files and depends on arbitrary operations such as symbol resolution, alias origins, assignability, AST ancestry, declaration enumeration, and `findReferencesAsNodes()`.

Upstream currently labels the native LSP “nearly complete,” but the general API is still **not ready**. Their 7.1 API roadmap explicitly lists `createProgram` and `createSourceFile` as missing pieces needed by tools such as `ts-morph`. [typescript-go status](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/blob/main/README.md), [API roadmap](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/issues/4830).

Where native LSP could help:

- `refs`, rename-like identity lookup, definitions, and perhaps targeted callers.
- Repeated interactive queries against one warm server.
- Avoiding repeated project construction for one-symbol navigation.

Where it currently does not fit:

- `columns`, `respell`, `regkeys`, `stringy`, brand analysis, schema twins, arbitrary AST classification, and custom graph construction.
- One-shot CLI runs where LSP startup and JSON-RPC transfer may erase the speed gain.
- In-memory planted controls, because the native API’s ad hoc program/source-file surface is still being built.

So I would **not migrate `pnpm ast` to LSP wholesale**. The right experiment is a narrow benchmark adapter for `refs`/identity callers against a persistent TS7 LSP, measuring cold start, warm query, memory, and result parity. If that wins, we can use LSP as a navigation accelerator while keeping `ts-morph` for semantic audits. TypeScript’s own guidance still recommends side-by-side native compilation and the older API for tooling that needs it. [TypeScript 7 progress](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/progress-on-typescript-7-december-2025/)

The dominant problem is repeated language-service reference search, multiplied by native worlds and by every value export.

Let:

- `F` = authored files,
- `P` = native programs,
- `E` = exported value declarations in package scope,
- `C(d)` = programs containing declaration `d`,
- `S(p)` = compiler graph size for program `p`,
- `R(d,p)` = references returned for `d` in `p`.

Current cost is approximately:

```text
load:       Θ(Σp S(p)) time and retained memory
enumerate:  Θ(F × P × membership-scan) plus export-map work
references: Θ(Σd∈E [P + Σp∈C(d) (S(p) + R(d,p))])
dedupe:     Θ(Σd references(d)) space, plus O(Ud log Ud) sort per declaration
```

`findReferencesAsNodes()` is implementation-dependent, but its worst-case search is program-wide. The important concrete fact is that it runs once per value export per containing native program.

- `collectTypeOnlyCandidates` visits every non-test in-scope file and every own export; no cheap candidate narrowing occurs before reference search: `tooling/src/ast/ops/typeonly.ts:157-171`.

- For each declaration, `findReferences`:
  - recomputes containing programs,

  - runs `findReferencesAsNodes()` in every containing program,
  - canonicalizes and deduplicates only after all searches have happened,
  - sorts the complete union: `ts-workspace.ts:180-197`.
- `containingPrograms` scans every program and asks each retained `Project` for the file on every declaration: `ts-workspace.ts:168-171`.
- Native programs are separate retained `Project`s. Each loads its roots, resolves dependencies, and remains cached: `ts-workspace.ts:66-76`, `79-97`. Shared sources therefore occupy memory once per native program graph.
